title: Daily life on horseback
hookLine: cooking, praying and reading the Granth in camps

lines: BEFORE DAWN IN A RIDERS' CAMP.
NOBODY KNOWS WHAT THE DAY HOLDS.
cards: Before dawn in a riders' camp. Horses stamping in the cold. Somebody blowing on last night's coals.

Nobody knows yet whether today means a long ride, a fight, or a day hiding in tall grass. And before any of that is decided, voices start up, low, among the tents and blankets: the morning prayers, said from memory.
The history books fill up with battles and sieges. Today is about the hours in between. Today: daily life on horseback.

teach.b: Start with the prayers, because tradition puts them first. Guru Ram Das left a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib about a Sikh's day.

In paraphrase: one who calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early, bathes, and remembers the Name, and keeps remembering it sitting and standing through the day. Notice what it needs. No building, no fixed address.
The riders could carry it anywhere, and tradition says they knew the daily prayers by heart. Second, the Granth itself.

teach.h: THE GRANTH OPENED WHEREVER THEY STOPPED.
teach.b: Tradition says the bands carried copies of the scripture, wrapped and kept with care, and when the camp stopped, a place was made for it, and it was opened and read, the way it is in a gurdwara.
A gurdwara, in a sense, could be pitched like a tent. Third, the food. Riders cooked what they could get: coarse bread, roasted grain, whatever a village shared.

teach.h: COOKED TOGETHER, EATEN ON THE GROUND.
teach.b: Tradition says even here it was cooked together and eaten together, sitting on the ground. Put the three side by side. The hunted years didn't stop Sikh practice.
They made it portable: the prayers in memory, the scripture in a bundle, the shared meal around whatever fire there was. When the camp moved, all of it moved too.

how: Sikhs say their daily prayers, the nitnem, morning, evening and night, often from memory or a small prayer book, wherever they are; at home, travel or work, the practice goes with them.

o: the morning prayers recited from memory
the scripture the riders carried with them
a riders' camp that moved from place to place

games.q: a day in the camp — tap the pairs.

s: with no gurdwaras to go to, the riders stopped reading the scripture
tradition says they carried copies and opened them wherever the camp stopped.
the daily prayers needed nothing but memory and a voice
that's why they could go anywhere a rider went.
riders always ate alone in the saddle
tradition says even in camp the food was cooked together and eaten together.

games.q: you're in a riders' camp before dawn. word might come any minute to break camp and ride hard. the morning prayers take time. what do you do?
o: skip them today and make them up when it's safe.
say them now, from memory, before anything else.
wait until you reach a gurdwara.
games.why: tradition says the riders kept the prayers first, from memory, wherever they were. Guru Ram Das's hymn asks a Sikh to rise early and remember the Name.

practice: If you can, move to a different spot: the step outside, a chair by a window, or just turn to face another wall. Settle there and do what you usually do, a breath, a line of prayer, Waheguru if you pray, or simple silence.
Notice how the place is different and the practice is the same.

wordCard.voice: Granth, the scripture the hunted riders carried wrapped and opened wherever the camp stopped. In the riders' camps, prayers said from memory, and food cooked and eaten together. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for nitnem, the daily round of Sikh prayers.

carryVoice: Your line: prayer on the move. It never needed a building, only a voice. See you tomorrow.
